question: Why do you want to study Botany specifically, rather than a broader biology degree?
lookingFor: A specific, genuine pull toward plant science rather than a generic love of biology.

bullets: Name the specific aspect of plant science that draws you, not biology in general
Give a concrete moment or experience that narrowed your interest to plants
Show awareness of what a Botany degree actually covers versus zoology or general life sciences
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've always found plants strange in a good way, they can't run from a threat or a drought so they've evolved these incredibly clever chemical and structural solutions instead, and that problem-solving is what pulls me in more than animal biology ever did. Growing my own chillies and tomatoes on our balcony got me reading about why some seedlings damped off and others thrived, which led me down a rabbit hole into soil microbiology and plant pathology. I want a degree that lets me go deep on that rather than skim plants as one unit among many in a general life sciences course.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I love nature' with nothing plant-specific
Not being able to distinguish Botany from general biology
Sounding like Botany was a fallback from Medicine
followUps: What part of plant science interests you least, and why?

question: Why do you want to study Botany at our university in particular?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the course, not just prestige or convenience.

bullets: Reference a specific module, herbarium, botanical garden, or research group
Connect that feature to a concrete interest or experience of yours
Avoid language generic enough to apply to any university
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read that your department runs its own botanical garden and that second-years get to design a small research project in it rather than just visiting on field trips, and that hands-on access is rare. I've been growing and cross-pollinating dwarf beans at home to see how traits sort in the next generation, so a course where I can actually run something similar with proper equipment and supervision felt like the natural next step. I also noticed your strength in plant pathology, which lines up with the disease resistance question I got interested in through my own failed seedlings.

commonMistakes: Citing only rankings or campus life
Naming a feature that doesn't actually exist in the course
Giving an answer that would fit any biology department
followUps: What would you want to research if you had that garden access?

question: What first got you interested in plants?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific origin story that shows sustained curiosity rather than a rehearsed line.

bullets: Give one real, specific moment or experience rather than a vague claim
Show how that early spark developed into something more sustained
Avoid a story that sounds manufactured for the interview
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My grandmother kept an allotment and I used to spend summers there as a kid, mostly just eating raspberries, but I remember being genuinely confused when she explained that the runner beans needed bees to visit the flowers or we'd get no pods at all. That one fact stuck with me, the idea that a plant's whole life cycle depends on this invisible negotiation with insects. It's part of why I ended up doing my school extended project on pollinator visits to different flower shapes in our school garden.

commonMistakes: A generic 'I've always loved nature' with no specifics
A story with no follow-through into later interest
Overly rehearsed, implausibly poetic phrasing
followUps: Has that early interest changed direction since then?

question: Tell us about any hands-on experience you have with plants, growing, fieldwork, or a related project.
lookingFor: Genuine practical engagement with plants and evidence of what you learned from it, not just a listed activity.

bullets: Describe one specific piece of hands-on work in enough detail to show you actually did it
Explain a problem you ran into and how you worked it out
Link it to what it taught you about plant biology or your own interests
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I volunteered for a term at a community garden restoring a neglected plot, and I ended up in charge of a bed that kept getting powdery mildew on the courgettes. I tried spacing the plants further apart and watering at the base instead of overhead, and the difference by August was obvious, which taught me more about fungal disease and airflow than any textbook chapter did. It also made me want to understand the biology behind why that worked, not just that it did.

commonMistakes: Listing an activity with no detail of what was actually done
No reflection on what was learned
Claiming expertise well beyond what the experience supports
followUps: What would you have done differently if you ran that project again?

question: What have you read outside the syllabus that deepened your interest in Botany?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with a specific source and the ability to discuss it critically, not just name-drop a title.

bullets: Name a specific book, paper, or article, not a vague genre
Explain one particular idea from it that stuck with you
Show some critical engagement, not just summary
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Peter Wohlleben's 'The Hidden Life of Trees', and while I enjoyed it, I actually went looking afterward for the primary research behind the mycorrhizal network claims because some of the language felt more emotive than the data seemed to support. That led me to Suzanne Simard's actual papers on carbon transfer between Douglas firs, which was a useful lesson that popular science and the underlying research can tell quite different versions of the same story. It made me more careful about checking sources before I repeat a claim.

commonMistakes: Naming a book without being able to discuss its content
No critical distance from the source, pure summary
Claiming to have read something clearly unfamiliar
followUps: Did anything in that reading challenge what you previously believed?

question: How would you explain the scope of Botany to someone who thinks it's just about gardening?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate sense of the breadth of plant science beyond horticulture.

bullets: Distinguish gardening as an applied skill from Botany as a scientific discipline
Mention at least two or three sub-areas, such as physiology, genetics, ecology, or pathology
Give a concrete example of a real research question in the field
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Gardening is really about applying known techniques to grow plants well, whereas Botany asks why those techniques work at a cellular and molecular level, and it stretches from plant genetics and physiology through to ecology and evolution. For example, botanists study how drought-tolerant genes could be bred into staple crops to cope with climate change, which has nothing to do with pruning roses but everything to do with feeding people. I'd say gardening is one small applied slice of a much bigger scientific field.

commonMistakes: Treating Botany and gardening as basically synonymous
Listing sub-areas with no example to ground them
Overly narrow definition limited to plant identification
followUps: Which sub-area of Botany interests you most?

question: Can you walk us through, in outline, what happens during photosynthesis?
lookingFor: A correct, clear outline of the light and light-independent reactions without needing exhaustive detail.

bullets: Identify the inputs (light, water, carbon dioxide) and outputs (glucose, oxygen)
Distinguish the light reactions in the thylakoid from the Calvin cycle in the stroma
Mention chlorophyll's role in capturing light energy
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In simple terms, chlorophyll in the chloroplast absorbs light energy and uses it in the thylakoid membranes to split water, releasing oxygen and generating ATP and NADPH. Those energy carriers are then used in the stroma during the Calvin cycle to fix carbon dioxide into sugars, essentially building glucose out of thin air using the sun as the power source. What I find genuinely elegant is that the whole process is really two separate factories, one capturing energy and one using it to build molecules, running side by side in the same organelle.

commonMistakes: Confusing photosynthesis with respiration
Omitting where in the cell the reactions occur
Vague hand-waving with no mention of inputs and outputs
followUps: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis if carbon dioxide is limited?

question: What's the difference between C3 and C4 plants, and why does it matter?
lookingFor: Understanding of the adaptive advantage of C4 photosynthesis in hot, dry conditions, not just the biochemical labels.

bullets: Explain that C4 plants fix carbon into a four-carbon compound first, concentrating carbon dioxide near the enzyme rubisco
State why this matters: it reduces photorespiration, especially in heat and low water availability
Give an example of each type, such as wheat versus maize or sugarcane
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: C3 plants, like wheat and rice, fix carbon dioxide directly into a three-carbon compound using rubisco, but in hot, dry conditions they have to close their stomata to save water, which lets oxygen build up and causes wasteful photorespiration. C4 plants such as maize and sugarcane get around this by first fixing carbon into a four-carbon compound in outer cells, then pumping it into specialised bundle sheath cells where it's concentrated before rubisco ever sees it, which suppresses photorespiration almost entirely. It's essentially an evolutionary workaround for hot climates, which is part of why C4 crops are getting so much attention for future food security.

commonMistakes: Reciting the names without explaining the functional advantage
Confusing C4 with CAM photosynthesis
No real-world example given
followUps: Why haven't all crop plants evolved C4 photosynthesis if it's so efficient?

question: What structures does a plant cell have that an animal cell doesn't, and what do they do?
lookingFor: Accurate recall of the key distinguishing structures with a functional explanation for each.

bullets: Name the cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole
Explain the functional role of each, not just the name
Show understanding of why these structures matter for a stationary, photosynthetic organism
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Plant cells have a rigid cellulose cell wall outside the membrane, which gives structural support and lets the plant stay upright without a skeleton. They also have chloroplasts, which is where photosynthesis actually happens, and a large central vacuole that manages water storage and turgor pressure, basically keeping the cell rigid by pushing outward against the wall. All three make sense together for an organism that can't move to find water or shelter and has to build its own food from sunlight.

commonMistakes: Naming a structure without explaining its function
Missing the central vacuole
Confusing cell wall with cell membrane
followUps: What happens to a plant cell's shape if it loses too much water?

question: What is transpiration and why is it important to a plant?
lookingFor: A correct definition plus understanding of why it matters beyond simple water loss.

bullets: Define transpiration as the loss of water vapour, mainly through stomata
Explain its role in pulling water and dissolved minerals up through the xylem
Mention its role in cooling the plant
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Transpiration is the evaporation of water vapour, mostly through the stomata on the underside of leaves, and it sounds like pure water loss but it's actually doing important work. As water evaporates from the leaf it creates a negative pressure that pulls more water and dissolved minerals up through the xylem from the roots, which is essentially how a tree moves water without any pump. It also helps cool the leaf, a bit like sweating does for us.

commonMistakes: Describing it as purely wasteful water loss
Not connecting it to xylem transport
Confusing transpiration with respiration
followUps: What environmental factors would increase the rate of transpiration?

question: Can you describe how auxin controls a plant's growth toward light?
lookingFor: Understanding of phototropism as an unequal auxin distribution problem, with correct directionality.

bullets: Identify auxin as the hormone responsible and where it's produced, the shoot tip
Explain that light causes auxin to move toward the shaded side of the shoot
Describe how higher auxin concentration causes cells to elongate more on that shaded side, bending the shoot toward the light
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Auxin is produced at the shoot tip and when light hits from one side, it triggers auxin to move laterally toward the shaded side rather than being distributed evenly. That side then has a higher auxin concentration, which makes those cells elongate more than the cells on the illuminated side, and because one side is growing faster than the other, the shoot physically bends toward the light. What I find satisfying about it is that it's not the plant sensing light and choosing to grow that way, it's a purely mechanical consequence of uneven hormone distribution.

commonMistakes: Saying the plant 'grows toward light' with no mechanism
Getting the direction of auxin movement backwards
Confusing phototropism with photoperiodism
followUps: How would you design an experiment to test this mechanism?

question: What's the difference between xylem and phloem?
lookingFor: Correct distinction between the two transport tissues, including direction of flow and what each carries.

bullets: State that xylem carries water and minerals upward from roots, in dead, hollow cells
State that phloem carries sugars produced by photosynthesis, up or down, in living cells
Note that xylem flow is one-directional while phloem can move in either direction depending on need
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals from the roots up to the rest of the plant, and it's made of dead, hollow, lignified cells that essentially form a passive pipe, so flow only goes one way, upward. Phloem, by contrast, carries sugars made during photosynthesis from wherever they're produced to wherever they're needed, whether that's up to a growing shoot tip or down to the roots for storage, and it's made of living cells because that movement takes active energy. I think of xylem as a one-way drinking straw and phloem as a more flexible delivery network.

commonMistakes: Mixing up which tissue carries water versus sugar
Not knowing phloem transport is bidirectional
Missing that xylem cells are dead
followUps: Why does phloem transport require living cells while xylem doesn't?

question: What distinguishes angiosperms from gymnosperms?
lookingFor: Correct core distinction (enclosed seeds and flowers versus exposed seeds) with an example of each.

bullets: State that angiosperms produce flowers and enclose their seeds in a fruit or ovary
State that gymnosperms produce naked seeds, typically in cones, with no flowers
Give a clear example of each group
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Angiosperms are the flowering plants, and their defining feature is that the seed is enclosed inside an ovary, which usually develops into a fruit, so think of something like an apple tree. Gymnosperms, like pine or spruce trees, produce what's called a naked seed, meaning it's not enclosed in an ovary, and instead it usually sits exposed on the surface of a cone scale. The flower and the enclosed seed are really the key evolutionary innovation that separates the two groups.

commonMistakes: Confusing gymnosperms with ferns or mosses
Unable to give a concrete example of either group
Missing that the seed enclosure is the defining feature, not just flowers
followUps: Why might an enclosed seed be an evolutionary advantage?

question: How do plants know what time of year it is in order to flower at the right moment?
lookingFor: Understanding of photoperiodism, the role of day length, and awareness of long-day versus short-day plants.

bullets: Explain that plants detect day length, or more precisely night length, using a photoreceptor pigment called phytochrome
Distinguish long-day and short-day plants and give an example of each
Note that this is what lets flowering align reliably with season rather than just temperature
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Plants track day length, or really the length of uninterrupted darkness, using a pigment called phytochrome that switches between two forms depending on the light it absorbs. Some species, called long-day plants like spinach, flower when nights get short enough in early summer, while short-day plants like chrysanthemums need nights to be longer than a critical length, so they flower in autumn. It's a more reliable cue than temperature alone because day length is exactly the same every year regardless of an unusually warm or cold spell.

commonMistakes: Saying plants simply respond to temperature
Confusing long-day and short-day definitions
Not mentioning phytochrome or any sensing mechanism at all
followUps: What would happen to a short-day plant if you interrupted its dark period with a flash of light?

question: How are plants classified, and why do botanists sometimes revise a species' classification?
lookingFor: Basic grasp of taxonomic hierarchy and awareness that classification is evidence-based and can change with new data.

bullets: Mention the taxonomic hierarchy, at least kingdom down to species, with binomial nomenclature
Note that classification was originally based on morphology and is increasingly based on DNA evidence
Explain why revisions happen, such as genetic evidence revealing a species is misplaced
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Plants are organised in a hierarchy from kingdom down through phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species, with each species given a two-part Latin name under the binomial system. Classification used to rely almost entirely on physical features like flower structure or leaf shape, but a lot of it is being revised now that we can compare DNA sequences directly, since two plants can look similar but be only distantly related, or look different but share a recent common ancestor. It's a reminder that taxonomy isn't a fixed filing system, it's a hypothesis about evolutionary relationships that gets updated as better evidence comes in.

commonMistakes: Treating classification as fixed and never revised
Not knowing the binomial naming convention
Confusing taxonomy with simple plant identification
followUps: Can you think of an example where DNA evidence changed how a group of organisms was classified?

question: What is a mycorrhizal relationship, and why is it significant for plants?
lookingFor: Correct understanding of the mutualism between fungi and plant roots and its practical significance.

bullets: Define mycorrhiza as a mutualistic association between fungi and plant roots
Explain the exchange: fungi extend the root's effective surface area for water and nutrient uptake, especially phosphorus, in return for sugars from photosynthesis
Mention a practical significance, such as improved drought tolerance or reduced need for fertiliser
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A mycorrhizal relationship is a mutualistic partnership between a fungus and a plant's roots, where the fungus's thread-like hyphae spread through the soil far beyond what the roots alone could reach, massively increasing the surface area available for absorbing water and nutrients like phosphorus. In exchange, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars from photosynthesis that it can't make for itself. It matters practically because mycorrhizal plants often cope better with drought and poor soils, which is part of why there's growing interest in using these fungi to reduce reliance on chemical fertiliser in agriculture.

commonMistakes: Describing it as parasitic rather than mutualistic
Not explaining what each partner gains
No mention of practical or agricultural relevance
followUps: Can you think of a downside or risk of a plant depending heavily on a fungal partner?

question: Can you describe an invasive plant species and explain why it's able to outcompete native plants?
lookingFor: A concrete example with a plausible ecological explanation, showing awareness of a real conservation issue.

bullets: Name a specific invasive species you can discuss with some detail
Explain a real mechanism for its success, such as lack of natural predators, faster growth, or allelopathy
Show awareness of the ecological or economic impact
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Japanese knotweed is one I looked into because it's such a problem in the UK, it can grow through concrete and spreads through tiny fragments of root, so even a small disturbed piece can start a new colony. Part of why it's so successful here is that it left its natural pests and diseases behind in Japan, so nothing here keeps its growth in check the way it would at home, and it also grows extremely fast, shading out native plants before they can establish. It's a good example of how an ecological problem, invasive spread, ends up being a legal and economic one too, since it can affect property values and mortgages in the UK.

commonMistakes: Naming a species with no real explanation of its success
Confusing invasive with simply non-native
No awareness of real-world consequences
followUps: What approaches could be used to control it, and what are the trade-offs?

question: What's your view on genetically modified crops? Should they play a bigger role in agriculture?
lookingFor: Balanced, evidence-aware reasoning that weighs benefits and concerns rather than a one-sided verdict.

bullets: Acknowledge genuine benefits, such as pest resistance, drought tolerance, or reduced pesticide use
Address genuine concerns, such as biodiversity loss, corporate control of seed, or public trust
Reach a reasoned, qualified position rather than an absolute stance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think GM crops have real potential, things like Bt cotton reducing insecticide use, or drought-tolerant maize varieties that could matter enormously as climate patterns shift. What gives me pause isn't really the science of gene editing itself, it's more the practical questions around seed patents concentrating control with a few large companies, and the risk of reducing crop genetic diversity if everyone plants the same engineered variety. My honest position is that GM technology should play a bigger role, but it needs to be paired with strong regulation and support for smallholder farmers, otherwise the benefits won't be shared fairly.

commonMistakes: A purely emotional 'GM is unnatural' argument with no evidence
Ignoring legitimate concerns and giving uncritical support
Refusing to commit to any actual position
followUps: How would you respond to someone who says GM crops are inherently unsafe to eat?

question: How is climate change affecting plant life, and can you give a specific example?
lookingFor: Concrete, specific understanding of a real climate impact on plants, not vague generalities.

bullets: Give a specific, real example of a climate-driven change in plants
Explain the underlying mechanism, not just the outcome
Show awareness of a wider consequence, ecological or agricultural
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: One example I find striking is the shift in flowering times, records going back over a century in the UK show many species now flower around a month earlier than they did in the 1950s, tracking rising spring temperatures. The mechanism is fairly direct, many plants use temperature as a cue alongside day length to trigger flowering, so warmer springs push that threshold earlier. What worries me is the mismatch it can create with pollinators that might not shift their timing at the same rate, so the plant and its pollinator can end up out of sync even though both are responding to the same warming climate.

commonMistakes: Vague statement that 'climate change harms plants' with no example
No mechanism given, just the observed effect
Confusing weather variability with long-term climate trends
followUps: What could a plant species do, evolutionarily or through migration, to cope with this shift?

question: Why does plant biodiversity matter, beyond the fact that plants are pleasant to look at?
lookingFor: A substantive argument covering ecological, practical, and scientific reasons for conserving plant diversity.

bullets: Cover ecological function, such as supporting food webs and ecosystem services like pollination or soil stability
Cover practical value, such as genetic resources for future crop breeding or medicine
Avoid resting the whole answer on aesthetics or vague sentiment
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Plant diversity underpins almost every ecosystem service we rely on, from the soil stability that prevents erosion to the pollination networks that depend on a range of flowering times and shapes, not just one crop. There's also a more practical argument, wild relatives of crops carry genetic traits like drought or disease resistance that we might urgently need for future breeding, and once a species is extinct that genetic library is gone permanently. I think of biodiversity loss less as losing something pretty and more as narrowing our options for solving problems we haven't even encountered yet.

commonMistakes: Answering purely in terms of aesthetics or sentiment
Only naming one reason instead of several distinct angles
Vague claims with no concrete mechanism or example
followUps: What's a real-world example of a wild plant relative being used to improve a crop?

question: Plants can't run away from herbivores. What strategies have they evolved to defend themselves?
lookingFor: A concrete grasp of both physical and chemical plant defences, ideally with a specific example.

bullets: Give at least one physical defence, such as thorns, trichomes, or tough leaves
Give at least one chemical defence, such as toxins, tannins, or induced volatile signalling
Ideally mention that defences can be constitutive or induced in response to actual damage
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Plants have both physical and chemical strategies. Physically, you get things like thorns on a rose or the fine hairs, called trichomes, on a tomato leaf that make it harder or less pleasant for an insect to feed. Chemically, a lot of plants store toxins or bitter compounds like tannins that discourage grazing, and some species go further and only ramp up production of these compounds after they've actually been damaged, which is called an induced response, and it can even include releasing volatile chemicals that attract the predators of the insect eating them. It's a genuinely clever arms race considering the plant can't move at all.

commonMistakes: Only naming physical defences with no chemical example
Treating all defences as constant rather than some being induced by damage
Vague 'plants protect themselves' with no concrete mechanism
followUps: Can you explain how a plant might 'call for help' when attacked by an insect?

question: Can you give some examples of how plants disperse their seeds, and why dispersal matters?
lookingFor: Clear knowledge of multiple dispersal mechanisms and an understanding of why dispersal is adaptively useful.

bullets: Give at least two distinct dispersal mechanisms with an example each, such as wind, animal, or water
Explain why dispersal away from the parent plant is advantageous
Connect a specific seed adaptation to its dispersal method
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Dandelion seeds have that feathery parachute structure so they can be carried on the wind, while something like a burdock seed has hooks that catch on animal fur to hitch a ride, and coconuts are buoyant enough to float across the ocean to a new island. Dispersal matters because seedlings that land right under the parent plant end up competing with it for the same light, water, and nutrients, and are more likely to be found by the same pests, so spreading out improves the odds that at least some offspring reach a favourable spot. It's a nice example of how a seed's physical structure directly reflects its dispersal strategy.

commonMistakes: Only naming one mechanism instead of several
Not explaining why dispersal itself is advantageous
Confusing dispersal with pollination
followUps: Why might a plant produce a very large number of small seeds instead of a few large ones?

question: Is there a piece of current botanical research or a discovery you find particularly exciting?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific engagement with real recent research, able to explain it and say why it matters.

bullets: Name a specific, real piece of research or discovery, not a vague trend
Explain the finding accurately in your own words
Say specifically why it excites you or what question it opens up
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been reading about work on using CRISPR to edit disease resistance genes directly into existing banana varieties, rather than breeding new ones from scratch, which matters because most commercial bananas are a single clone with almost no genetic diversity to resist disease naturally. What excites me is that it sidesteps the usual multi-decade breeding timeline entirely, since you're editing the plant we already grow rather than starting from a wild relative and crossing for years. It raises a genuinely interesting question for me about how quickly gene editing could reshape crop security compared to traditional breeding, which I'd love to actually study properly.

commonMistakes: A vague reference to 'genetic engineering' with no specific example
Unable to explain the finding accurately when pressed
Enthusiasm with no real understanding behind it
followUps: What's a concern or limitation of that approach that you're aware of?

question: Where do you hope studying Botany will take you, career-wise?
lookingFor: A grounded, honestly reasoned direction connected to real interests, not an implausibly precise plan.

bullets: Give a genuine direction of interest rather than an exact job title carved in stone
Connect that direction to something specific you've already engaged with
Show openness to the degree shaping or changing that direction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I'm drawn toward plant pathology and crop resilience, partly from my own struggles keeping a vegetable patch disease-free, and partly because food security feels like one of the most concrete ways plant science actually matters to people's lives. I don't think I'll know exactly what that looks like as a career until I've done more research myself, whether that's in a lab, in the field, or somewhere more policy-facing, and I'm genuinely open to the course changing my mind. What I am sure of is that I want to spend my working life asking questions about how plants function and how to help them cope with a harder climate.

commonMistakes: An unrealistically specific ten-year plan with no room for change
A goal with no connection to actual experience or interest
Sounding indifferent about where the degree leads
followUps: What's a career path in Botany you'd rule out, and why?

question: A rare native orchid population is found growing on land earmarked for a housing development that a struggling community badly needs. How would you think through that conflict?
lookingFor: Structured reasoning that takes both conservation and human need seriously, rather than a snap verdict either way.

bullets: Acknowledge genuine value on both sides rather than dismissing either
Consider concrete options short of an all-or-nothing choice, such as relocation, seed banking, or redesigned siting
Reach a reasoned position while being honest about what would be lost
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My instinct isn't to treat it as orchid versus houses, because that framing throws away better options. I'd want to know first whether the population could realistically be propagated or relocated, since many orchids depend on specific mycorrhizal fungi in the soil that make transplanting genuinely difficult, so that's not automatically a clean solution. If relocation genuinely isn't viable and it's truly one of the last populations, I'd lean toward protecting it and pushing hard for the development to be redesigned around that specific patch of land, because an extinction is irreversible in a way that a delayed or reshaped housing project isn't. But I'd want to be honest that this has a real cost for people who need homes, and I wouldn't pretend that trade-off away.

commonMistakes: An easy 'save the orchid' answer with no acknowledgement of the human cost
Dismissing the conservation concern as unimportant compared to housing
Refusing to reach any actual position
followUps: Would your answer change if the orchid population were common rather than rare?
